lesson.title: Capstone: Build Your Own DNS Resolver
lesson.summary: This capstone has you implement a working, simplified DNS system, from a resolver that walks the delegation chain from root to authoritative server, through a caching layer, to an optional DNSSEC validation step, demystifying the lookup that happens before nearly every network connection.
lesson.body:
Every time you type a domain name into a browser, a lookup happens before a single byte of the actual page can be requested. This capstone asks you to build the machinery behind that lookup yourself, rather than relying on your operating system to do it invisibly. The core deliverable is a recursive resolver: given a domain name, it performs the full walk from the root of the DNS hierarchy down to the server that actually knows the answer, and returns the result. As a stretch goal, you can also build a tiny authoritative server that answers queries for a zone you define yourself, so you see both sides of a DNS conversation.

Start by writing code that hardcodes the address of a root server and sends it a query for the domain you are trying to resolve. A root server will not know the final answer, but it will refer you to the name servers responsible for the relevant top level domain, for example the servers responsible for .com. Your code then queries one of those, which in turn refers you further down, to the authoritative name servers for the specific domain. Only at that last step do you get an actual answer, such as the IP address behind a hostname. Walking through resolving something like www.example.com by hand this way, one referral at a time, makes concrete something that is normally completely hidden: a single lookup can involve several separate queries to several different servers before it produces an answer, all of it happening in the recursive resolver so that the end user or application never has to think about any of it.

This project deliberately exercises the DNS record types and hierarchy covered earlier: A and AAAA records mapping names to addresses, NS records pointing to name servers, and CNAME records aliasing one name to another, all of which your resolver needs to understand and follow correctly. It also exercises DNS caching directly, and this is where the project becomes genuinely instructive rather than just an exercise in following referrals. Every DNS record comes with a TTL, a time to live, telling anyone who receives it how long they are allowed to keep and reuse that answer before asking again. Build a cache keyed by the domain name and record type, and honor each entry's TTL by expiring it at the right time. Once your cache is working, resolve the same domain twice in a row and watch the second lookup skip almost the entire walk down the hierarchy, answered instantly from memory instead. That difference is exactly why real world DNS caching matters at internet scale: without it, the small number of root and top level domain servers would be overwhelmed by repeated queries for the same popular domains.

As a further extension, consider DNSSEC. Ordinary DNS answers are not authenticated in any cryptographic sense, which means a resolver has no built in way to know an answer has not been tampered with somewhere along its path. DNSSEC adds a chain of digital signatures, starting from a trusted root and extending down through each delegation, that a resolver can verify to confirm an answer is genuine. Implementing even a single signature verification step, rather than the full chain, teaches a great deal about why DNSSEC, despite solving a real and important problem, has been slow to deploy everywhere: every link in the delegation chain has to correctly sign its records and every resolver in the chain has to correctly validate them, and a single weak link anywhere breaks the guarantee.

By the end of this project you will have personally sent every kind of query involved in resolving a domain name, built the cache that makes repeated lookups fast, and grappled directly with why authenticating those answers is hard. Something you have relied on thousands of times without a second thought becomes something you can explain, and defend, from the root server down.
